how-to-price-junk-removal.html.text:
JUNK REMOVAL PRICING

How to price a junk removal job without giving the dump ticket away.

The search phrase is usually “junk removal cost calculator.” Almost every result is a lead form that asks for a zip code and a phone number. This page is the method behind a number you can stand on, and it pairs with a free browser calculator that does the arithmetic locally.

The landfill does not care how full the truck looks

Customers think in rooms and truck fractions. Transfer stations think in tons. Loose mixed household junk often lands around 150–250 pounds per cubic yard. The same yard of concrete is closer to two tons. Quote both as “half a truck” and one job prints a $45 minimum ticket while the other prints a $400 ticket. The driveway photograph cannot tell you which.

Build the ticket first

Estimate pounds from each pile (volume × a density you have actually seen on your tickets, or a count × typical item weight). Convert to tons. The dump charge is the greater of the landfill’s per-ton rate and its minimum ticket, plus any environmental surcharge, plus the special fees many sites charge for appliances, mattresses, and tires. That sum is the part of the job you cannot negotiate after the scale.

Then price the carry

On-site clock time, plus stairs, plus a long carry from the back yard, plus the round-trip drive, plus each dump run. Multiply by crew size. A two-person crew sitting in traffic is two wages, and a load that will not fit the trailer is a second dump run you did not quote. Payroll burden — employer tax, workers’ compensation, liability — belongs on the wage. Fuel is its own line.

Walk-away is cost, not the special

Overhead as a share of direct cost, then a target margin as a share of price, is how the customer number is built. A posted minimum (“$149 to roll the truck”) is a floor on that number. It is not a substitute for knowing cost. If a half-truck special is $199 and the ticket plus loaded labor is $230, the special is a donation. Hold the walk-away and let the customer decide whether the pile is worth it.

What this is not

Not a quote on your behalf, not a landfill tariff, not legal or business advice. Densities and fees vary by region, by how wet the load is, and by what the scale actually prints. Verify every figure against your own tickets before you send a price.

Open the junk removal bid calculator — it stays in your browser.

Common questions

How do junk removal companies charge?

Many advertise by the fraction of a truck. Transfer stations usually bill by the ton, with a minimum ticket and extra fees for appliances, mattresses, and tires. A volume quote that ignores weight underprices heavy debris.

How much does junk removal cost per cubic yard?

There is no single number. Mixed household junk is often a few hundred pounds per cubic yard; concrete can be around two tons per yard. Price per yard is the bid divided by volume after the dump ticket and labor are known, not a starting rate.

Why do half-truck specials lose money?

A posted special assumes a light mixed load and one dump run. Stairs, a long carry, a second dump, or a yard of concrete can put the dump ticket and loaded labor above the special before anyone is paid.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice. You are responsible for reviewing every number before relying on it.

FOR INDEPENDENT JUNK HAULERS

Price the dump ticket, not the truck.

A half-truck of couches and a half-truck of concrete look the same in the driveway. The landfill bills the weight. This calculator turns each pile into estimated tons, prices the ticket (minimum, per-ton, surcharge, appliance fees), then adds crew time, stairs, travel, and the dump run so you see the walk-away number before you quote the job.

The load

One row per material. Pounds per unit is a starting density — replace it with a figure from your own scale tickets. Quantity is cubic yards for bulk, or a count for appliances, mattresses, and tires.

MaterialQuantityLb / unitSpecial fee

Dump and truck

Transfer stations bill the greater of the per-ton rate and a minimum ticket, then often add an environmental or host-community surcharge. Appliance, mattress, and tire fees are on each row because many landfills will not take those on the regular ticket.

Labor and costs

On-site hours are clock time. Stairs, a long carry, round-trip drive, and each dump run are added, then multiplied by crew size so windshield time is loaded labor. A posted minimum lifts the customer’s number; it does not change the walk-away cost.

Where the dump ticket goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting densities and special fees are common ballpark figures, not a landfill tariff or a guarantee — weigh a few of your own loads and replace them. Read how to price a junk removal job.

    Common questions

    Why price by weight when customers ask for "a half truck"?

    Because the landfill bills the weight, not the picture of the truck. Two cubic yards of concrete at roughly 4,000 lb per yard outweigh a whole trailer of couches at about 125. This tool estimates weight from the material you enter, converts it to tons, and prices the dump ticket from your own per-ton rate, minimum, and surcharge — then the truck-volume question is answered separately, because volume decides how many trips you make, not what the scale house charges.

    Why enter each material as its own pile?

    Because a blended "mixed load" rate hides the dump ticket. Mixed household junk starts around 200 lb per cubic yard, furniture 125, construction debris 400, drywall 420, yard waste 350, dirt 2,200, concrete 4,000, and shingles 2,500. One heavy pile inside an otherwise light load is what turns a fine-looking bid into a loss at the scale. Appliances, mattresses, and tires are entered per item instead, because they carry a fixed special fee as well as weight.

    How are the number of dump runs worked out?

    From volume, not weight: total cubic yards divided by your truck capacity, rounded up, with a minimum of one run whenever there is anything to haul. Each run adds its own clock time, so a job that fits in one load and a job that needs three are priced as the different days they are. Weight drives the ticket; volume drives the trips. Getting those two the wrong way round is the single most common error in this trade's pricing.

    Does the calculator account for stairs and a long carry?

    Yes, both as their own clock time on top of the on-site hours you enter: minutes per flight multiplied by the number of flights, plus a long-carry allowance for the walk from the pile to the truck. That time is then multiplied by crew size to get person-hours, which is what payroll actually costs. A third-floor walk-up with a hundred-foot carry is not the same job as a curbside pile of the same volume, and this is where that difference shows up.

    Why does a small pickup still price at the minimum charge?

    Because rolling a truck costs more than the pile. Round-trip drive time from your one-way minutes, the dump-run time, fuel, and the landfill's own minimum all land before a single item is lifted. When the margin price comes in under the floor you set, the floor is used instead and the result says so. That number is what a "can you just grab this one couch?" call actually costs you.

    Why isn't a 20% margin the same as adding 20% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price — price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin) — which is how the quote reads to the customer and how your books read it. Overhead is a separate markup on direct cost, applied before margin and never to itself or to profit. A $400 cost marked up 20% is $480, a 16.7% margin; a 20% target margin is $500. Nothing leaves your browser: no account, no upload, business details for the printed proposal are cleared by "Forget my business details", and the optional local counter records only which features were used and the day. A share link encodes only the job details you see on screen into the web address itself, so copying one and sending it does not upload anything either.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

vs-a-flat-truck-fraction-rate.html.text:
← Junk Removal Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat truck-fraction rate

"$400 for a half truck" is not a price for a load — it is a price for whatever the rate happened to be built on, quietly applied to every pile that fills the same fraction of the truck.

What a flat truck-fraction rate is

A flat truck-fraction rate is the fastest way to quote a cleanout over the phone: ask how much of the truck it fills, quote a number for a quarter, half, or full truck, and skip the walkthrough. Customers shop it because it is easy to compare between haulers, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of load — usually mixed household junk and furniture — and then reused for every pile afterward, whether or not the next pile has concrete, dirt, drywall, or shingles mixed into it.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each material pile separately (mixed household junk, furniture, construction debris, drywall, yard waste, dirt, concrete, roofing shingles, or per-item appliances, mattresses, and tires), your dump fee per ton, minimum ticket, and surcharge, plus your own labor, stairs, travel, and target margin. It prices the estimated tonnage and dump ticket by material, then adds loaded labor and dump runs, and returns the bid price, the price per cubic yard, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money at the scale — for this pile, not a generic truck fraction.

What a flat truck-fraction rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a half truck of couches and a half truck of concrete — even though concrete alone runs roughly 4,000 lb per cubic yard against about 200 for mixed household junk. Prices each material's estimated tonnage separately, so a load with dense material in it costs more than the same volume of light junk.
Has no line for appliances, mattresses, or tires, regardless of how many special-fee items are in the pile. Prices appliance, mattress, and tire fees per item, on top of their own weight.
Estimates the truck fraction by eye, with no separate check against the landfill's own minimum ticket or surcharge. Prices the dump ticket as the greater of the per-ton rate and the minimum, plus your surcharge percent, so a light load still covers the ticket floor.
Has no line for stairs, a long carry, or a second dump run once the truck fills, regardless of how many the job needs. Prices stairs and long-carry minutes as loaded labor and adds clock time for every dump run the volume requires.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat truck-fraction rate would have quoted the same load, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two loads, the same truck fraction

Using this calculator's own shipped starting example:

An 11 cubic yard load of mixed household junk, furniture, and two appliances prices at $424.71 — $38.61 per cubic yard, on a job that costs $318.53 to run.

Load the same 11 cubic yards with a concrete tear-out instead, and the job costs $1,993.93 to run before a dollar of profit — almost entirely the dump ticket, which alone comes to $1,573.00 once 22 tons of concrete are billed at the per-ton rate. Applying the mixed-junk load's own $38.61-per-cubic-yard rate to this load quotes it at $424.71, the identical number, because both loads fill the same half of the truck.

That flat rate prices the concrete job $1,569.21 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $2,233.86 it falls short of this calculator's own bid price at a 25% target margin. Same truck fraction, same flat rate, one load that pays and one that loses money the moment the scale ticket prints.

Common questions

Why does a flat truck-fraction rate get a junk-removal quote wrong?

Because the cost driver at the scale house is weight, not the fraction of the truck the pile fills. A half truck of concrete or dirt weighs many times what a half truck of couches and boxes weighs, and the landfill bills the difference in tons, not in truck fractions. A flat half-truck or full-truck rate charges both loads the same.

What does a flat truck-fraction rate usually leave out entirely?

The material itself. A truck-fraction rate has no line for concrete, dirt, drywall, or roofing shingles weighing far more per cubic yard than mixed household junk or furniture, and no line for the appliance, mattress, and tire fees many landfills charge on top of the regular ticket.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own worked example: an 11 cubic yard load of mixed household junk, furniture, and two appliances prices at $424.71, or $38.61 per cubic yard. Applying that same $38.61 rate to an 11 cubic yard load that is a concrete tear-out instead quotes $424.71 -- $1,569.21 below that job's own $1,993.93 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit or the crew's time is covered. The flat rate does not just cut the margin on the concrete job; it prices it as a heavy loss.

Is a flat truck-fraction rate ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- household junk and furniture, no unusually dense material -- a truck-fraction rate can land close, because that is the material the rate was probably built on. The risk is applying it to a load with concrete, dirt, drywall, or shingles mixed in without separating that material out first, because the rate does not know what filled the truck and neither does the estimator until the load is already on the scale.

Does this calculator know what the dump charges or what labor costs in my market?

No. It has no data on your local landfill's rates or your local labor market. It takes the material and volume of each pile, your dump fee per ton, minimum ticket, and surcharge, plus your own labor, travel, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat truck-fraction rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Junk Removal Bid Calculator to price your own load, or read how to price a junk removal job.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify every figure against your own dump tickets, payroll, insurance, and fuel costs, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

Free and open source. If it keeps you off a losing half-truck special, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Workiz?

They do different jobs, and a hauling company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Workiz is a field service management platform, founded in 2015 by Idan Kadosh, Erez Marom, and Saar Kohanovitch and headquartered in San Diego, California, used by junk removal, locksmith, carpet cleaning, garage door, appliance repair, and other on-demand trades to run scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, and communication across a business, sold as an ongoing subscription account. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from each material pile's volume and density, plus appliance, mattress, and tire special fees, it estimates the tonnage the landfill will bill, then adds loaded labor for stairs and long carries, drive time, dump runs, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the bid price, the price per cubic yard, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money at the scale — before any of it touches a business-management system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A hauling company that already schedules crews, dispatches trucks, and invoices across every job is better served by Workiz or a comparable field service platform; a hauler who wants an instant, private answer to what one cleanout should cost from its material weight before opening a business system is in the right place here.
